topic: The anchoring trick stores use on you
title: The Pricing Trick Stores Use on You
voiceover: Stores show you a number first. Here's why. It's the anchoring effect. In 1974, Tversky and Kahneman had people watch a rigged wheel land on either 10 or 65. Then they asked: what percent of African countries are in the United Nations? People who saw 10 guessed around 25 percent. People who saw 65 guessed around 45. A random number pulled the guesses. That's anchoring: your first number quietly shapes everything after it. Stores use it with a high 'original price' next to the sale price so the deal feels bigger. Before you shop or negotiate, decide your own number first. What's it worth to you? Then compare. In a negotiation, making the first offer often sets the anchor. Tomorrow: why walking through a doorway can make you forget everything.

description: The first number you see quietly shapes your later judgments, which is why stores show a high original price next to the sale price. This is called anchoring. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), 'Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases', Science.
accuracy_note: Anchoring is one of the more robust effects in judgment research, though effect sizes vary by task. Figures are medians from the original wheel-of-fortune experiment (about 25% vs about 45%). Some later 'arbitrary anchor' studies (e.g. the Social Security number version) have had mixed replication, so we stick to the classic study.
